opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a question I kept asking myself: what is vision actually *for*?

For a long time in computer vision, especially in generative modeling, which is where I spent most of my research years, we were doing remarkable things. We could generate images that looked real, edit faces, synthesize 3D scenes, and later make video. Each year the quality jumped. But at some point I felt the excitement was increasingly about producing pixels for humans to look at. The output of the system was content, and the consumer of that content was a person scrolling on a screen.

That's valuable, but it's a closed loop inside the digital world. The model sees pixels and produces pixels. Nothing in the physical world changes because of it. And when I think about biological vision, that's not why eyes evolved. Animals didn't develop vision to make pictures. They developed it to act: find food, avoid danger, move through space, manipulate objects. Perception exists to serve action.

So I started to feel that if vision stays only in the digital world, it's capped. You can make the images more beautiful and the videos longer and more consistent, but the marginal value to society starts to flatten. Meanwhile, the physical world, with manufacturing, homes, logistics, and care work, is enormous, and our intelligent systems barely touch it.

There was also a technical reason. Many of the hardest open problems in vision, like real 3D understanding, physical dynamics, and how objects respond when you push them, are things you can't fully learn from passively watching internet data. You need interaction. A robot gives vision a body, and with a body you get feedback. You find out whether your understanding of the world is correct, because if it's wrong, the cup falls.

And honestly, the work we'd been doing in generative models and world models turned out to be a natural bridge. If you can model how a scene evolves over time, that is very close to what a robot needs in order to plan. So it didn't feel like abandoning vision. It felt more like taking vision to where it was always supposed to go.

r001.rationale: The response says digital-world vision applications have diminishing societal value, but it does not state that few applications beyond facial recognition and autonomous driving achieved massive scale or strong industrial value.

fable-5.1.text:
I wouldn't say I thought vision's potential was limited in an absolute sense. It's more that I started to feel the ceiling of what vision alone could do had become very visible, and the parts that still excited me all pointed outside the screen.

Think about where computer vision had gotten to. Recognition, detection, segmentation, generation, image and video synthesis. By the time I'd spent several years on generative models, you could produce almost any picture you wanted. And the honest question I kept asking myself was: what is this for? A model that can generate a beautiful image or a short video is valuable, sure, for entertainment, for design, for content. But the consumption of that output is still a human looking at a screen. The loop closes inside the digital world. The pixels don't do anything.

What bothered me more was something about the nature of the problem. In the digital world, the data is already there, and the task is largely about understanding or re-synthesizing it. That's a kind of passive intelligence. You're interpreting the world, not acting in it. And I became convinced that a lot of what we call understanding in vision models is actually quite shallow precisely because the model never has to pay a price for being wrong. If a generated video has a cup floating through a table, the loss is slightly higher. In the physical world, that same mistake means a broken cup, or a dropped object, or a failed task. Physics is a very strict teacher. I wanted that teacher.

There was also a practical realization. The big leap in language came when models started being used for things, when they became agents instead of just chat. For vision, the analogous leap isn't a better image generator. It's a system that perceives, reasons, and then changes the physical state of the world. That is robotics. So in a way I didn't feel like I was leaving vision. I felt like robotics is where vision actually gets to finish the sentence. Perception was always supposed to serve action; we just spent a decade building the first half.

And honestly, the timing mattered. Three or four years ago, the perception side was the bottleneck for robots, so a vision person going into robotics would have spent all their time fixing cameras and detectors. Now perception and generation are good enough that the interesting problem has shifted to the embodied side: how you turn visual understanding into reliable actions, how you learn from interaction, how you build world models that are grounded in consequences rather than in pixels. That's a problem where a vision background is useful but no longer sufficient, and that gap is exactly where I wanted to work.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses image generation and the limits of screen-based applications, but does not state that few computer-vision applications beyond facial recognition and autonomous driving had reached massive scale with strong industrial value.

astra-6.text:
For me, it wasn’t that computer vision had stopped being useful. It was that, in the digital world, you could understand an image or generate one, but you still needed something else to turn that result into an action. That made me think about how perception could have a more direct impact.

Robotics was interesting because it connects perception with action in the physical world. A robot needs to understand its surroundings, decide what to do, and then learn from what actually happens. Vision becomes part of that whole loop. So the attraction was less about leaving computer vision behind and more about taking it further—from interpreting visual information to using it to accomplish physical tasks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perception-to-action in robotics but does not state that few computer-vision applications beyond facial recognition and autonomous driving had reached massive scale with strong industrial value.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was less that computer vision had limited potential and more that I wanted to close the loop between perception and action. In the digital world, you can build a system that understands an image or generates beautiful content, but its impact often stays on a screen. Robotics raises another question: once a system understands what’s around it, can it actually do something useful?

That was the attraction. Vision becomes part of a larger system that has to make decisions, interact with its environment, and learn from what happens. Of course, that also makes the problem much harder. You have to deal with physical constraints and the consequences of mistakes. But the possibility of turning visual intelligence into useful action made it a direction I wanted to explore.

r001.rationale: The response says digital vision’s impact often stays on a screen, but does not state that few applications beyond facial recognition and autonomous driving achieved massive scale with strong industrial value.
